newsitem.title: INDIA: OPINION - MONETARY & CREDIT POLICY - APRIL 1997.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - MONETARY & CREDIT POLICY - APRIL 1997.

text.p: Kudos To RBI - What More Can One Ask For? - ICICI Securities
HIGHLIGHTS:
* CRR/SLR on inter-bank liabilities to go
* 10 percent CRR imposed on foreign deposits
* Bank Rate to emerge as an important reference rate, maximum deposit rate at 9 percent.
* All gilts/treasury bills made eligible for repos
* General Refinance Facility introduced
* MPBF scrapped, loan component increased
* Authorised dealers permitted to borrow/invest in overseas money markets.
* Authorised dealers to run FX swap book
* Bonds, debentures and preference shares outside 5 percent limit for bank investments
* Minimum tenure of Commercial Paper reduced to 30 days
ON A SILVER PLATTER.....

The euphoria created by the Union Budget has certainly been maintained by the Monetary Policy announced for the first half of 1997/98, and thankfully, Monetary Policy is insulated from the vagaries on the political front. Framed against the backdrop of strong monetary and deposit growth, rising inflation and extremely poor credit off-take (incremental credit/deposit ratio of 30 percent), the Governor's task has not been very easy. The threefold objective of the Policy is:
* Boost availability of credit to the industrial sector in order to spur real growth.
* Maintain price stability by contaning monetary expansion within 15-15.5 percent and inflation at around 6 percent.
* Further development of fixed income markets and closer integration between forecx and money markets.

The provisions of the Policy are aimed at driving lending rates lower and giving more freedom to banks as far as asset/liability composition of their balance sheet is concerned. Also, very evident from the Monetary Policy is RBI's concern about more than comfortable foreign currency reserves position as well as the strong capital inflows seen since March 1997.
LIABILITY SIDE IMPACT:
BANK RATE COMES OF AGE......

Market's thirst for a benchmark rate has been more than quenched with RBI elevating the stature of the near defunct "Bank Rate" to an all important reference rate. This has now become a very versatile signalling device which will be used by the Reserve Bank to indicate its stance on a wide range of monetary developments. The Bank Rate which had been immune to various structural changes in the market, fixed at 12 percent since October 1991, has now been changed to 11 percent.
* Interest rate on domestic term deposits for maturities from 30 days to one year has been capped at Bank Rate minus two percentage points. Hence, this rate now stands reduced from 10 to 9 percent.
* Interest rate offered on NRE term deposits for maturities from six months to one year has been capped at Bank Rate minus two percentage points.

* The interest rate on export credit refinance has been fixed at Bank Rate, amount of refinance being to the extent of 100 percent of incremental export credit outstanding over February 16, 1996 figures.

* In order to move away from sector-specific refinance facilities, RBI has introduced a General Refinance Facility to the extent of a bank's fortnightly average deposits in 1996/97. This facility would be available in two blocks of four weeks each. The interest rate on the first four weeks would be equal to Bank Rate and for the next four weeks at Bank Rate plus one percentage point. Beyond eight weeks, the current account balance of the bank would be debited by the quantum of refinance availed of. The amount of refinance available to banks under this facility will be to the extent of 46,000 million rupees.

* The liquidity support provided to Primary Dealers through repo transactions with RBI in 91 day treasury bills and dated securities was earlier at 10.5 percent and 11 percent respectively. The interest rate on this liquidity support has now been set at Bank Rate.
WITHDRAWAL OF CRR ON INTER-BANK LIABILITIES:

Inter-bank liabilities (net of inter-bank assests) were subject to a cash reserve ratio of 10%. These liabilities have now been exempt from maintenance of cash reserve requirements. More important than augmenting banks resources by Rs.950 crore through this provision, is the long term implication it will have on development of an active inter-bank term money market. The scientific price discovery of cost of money will improve the asset-liability management mechanism of banks, lead to the development of any yield curve for rupee funds and closer integration between domestic money markets and foreig exchange markets. The development of an onshore interest rate swap market should not be too far away.

In line with withdrawal of CRR on inter-bank liabilities, SLR also stands withdrawn. However, with banks' holding roughly Rs.20,000 crore of SLR assets in excess os statutory requirements, no significant impact is foreseen on the markets.
REIMPOSITION OF CASH RESERVE RATIO ON NON-RESIDENT DEPOSITS:

Needless to say, strong capital inflows seen over the past six months have been the underlying reason for reimposing CRR (10%) on incremental foreign deposits. The past couple of years have shown that CRR on foreign deposits has been used as a dynamic tool to regulate capital inflows from this front and will continue to be so. The flesibility with which CRR on non-resident deposits has been used has adequately reflected RBI's need to encourage or discourage such deposits.
GREATER FLEXIBILITY FOR BANKS IN FIXING INTEREST RATES OF NON-RESIDENT DEPOSIT:

Interest rates on FCNR(B) deposits which were earlier fixed by the Reserve Bank will now only be capped by the RBI. Interest rates on NRE term deposits have been freed for maturities greater than a year and those for maturities between six months and a year capped at Bank Rate minus two percentage points. These provisions will provide greater flexibility to banks in fine tuning the composition of their non-residental liabilites.
ASSET SIDE IMPACT
A CATALYST TO DEVELOPMENT OF THE REPO MARKET:

The scope of repo transactions which, apart from treasury bills was restricted to only certain specified government securities has now been extended to all government securities. This will increase the amount of repoable dated securities from Rs.81,611 crore to Rs.184,181 crore. Additionally, non-bank entities having an SGL account with Reserve Bank have been permitted to enter into repo transactions as lenders of money.
14 DAY, 28 DAY, 182 DAY TREASURY BILLS???

With the discontinuance of "ad-hoc" and "tap" treasury bill issuances, the Reserve Bank has expressed urgent need to introduce treasury bill issuances of various maturities. 14 day, 28 day and 182 day tenors seem to be the most likely ones. Shorter maturity treasury bills will help to improve cash management mechanisms of corporates and they will be able to park their short term surpluses in these instruments.
EXCLUSIVE 5% LIMIT FOR BANK INVESTMENT IN EQUITIES:

Banks were permitted to invest upto 5% of theor incremental deposits in shares and debentures of private sector corporates. This 5% limit is now exclusively for investment in equity shares. More important than the exclusivity given for equity shares is the fact that cap on investment in bonds, debentures and preference share has been removed. This is likely to lead to a spurt in issuances of corporate debentures and preference share as well as increased investment by banks in these instruments. The computation of Credit/Deposit ratio now needs to be amended to take into account banks investment in corporate debentures as well.

While this change augurs very well for corporate issuers, it deals a body blow to financial institutions and PSUs who were enjoying exclusively outside the 5% limit. This provision brings corporate issuers on par with DFI/PSU issuers as far as the largest investor segment banks, is concerned. DFIs/PSUs will now need to compete with pr;ivate sector corporates for the same pool of funds, and may not be able to command a significantly lower rate than some of the AAA corporate names. The credit differential spreads between DFI/PSU debt and corporate debt are expected to tighten as a result of this provision.
MINIMUM MATURITY OF COMMERICAL PAPER REDUCED:

The minimum maturity of Commerical Paper issuance has been reduced from three months to 30 days. This provision will enable corporates to raise short term funds at lower rates of interest. With shorter maturity treasury bills round the corner the reduced maturity is likely to be introduced to issuances of Certificates of Deposit as well.
CONSORTIUM LENDING NORMS EASED:

The threshold limit of Rs.50 crore for forming a consortium to fund working capital requirements of corporates has been eliminated. Hence banks will now have greater flexibility in credit delivery and can extend credit entirely on their own for sums exceeding Rs.50 crore. Alternatively, banks have the freedom to adopt the syndication route, irrespective of the amount of credit inolved.
LOAN COMPONENT RAISED, MPBF SCRAPPED:

All instructions relating to Maximu8m Permissible Bank Finance (MPBF) have been withdrawn. Banks now have complete flexibility to evolve methods to assess the working capital requirements of borrowers within the existing prudential norms and exposure limits.

For borrowers having an assessed working capital requirement of Rs.20 crore and above, the loan component has been increased from 75% to 80%. The loan component for borrowers with a working capital requirement of less than Rs.20crore but more than Rs.10 crore has been increased from 60% -75%. To ease the pressure on borrowers, the minimum period of loan can be fixed by banks and banks may also permit borrowers to invest their short term surpluses in money market instruments.
LENDING NORMS TO NBFCs RELAXED:

The existing restrictions on bank advances to NBFCs(in multiples of their net owned funds) have been removed in respect of those NBFCs which comply with registration, credit rating and prudential norms set by the RBI. Though banks are now free to decide the level of credit to such NBFCs, strict internal credit controls will need to be imposed by the lending banks to minimise their risks.
BANKS PERMITTED TO EXTEND LOANS AGAINST SHARES:

Empathising with the current state of the equity capital markets, RBI has allowed banks to extend loans to corporates against shares held by them in order to enable these corporates to meet their promoter contrinutions to equity of new companies. Such loans will be treated as banks investment in equity shares under the 5% limit.
FOREIGN EXCHANGE MARKETS:
AUTHORISED DEALERS GIVEN GREATER OPERATIONAL FREEDOM:

In order to bring about closed integration between overseas and domestic money markets, authorised dealers have been permitted to borrow from and invest in overseas money markets upto US$ 10 million through their overseas offices. This will even out arbitrage opportunities available between domestic and overseas money markets since authorised dealers have access, albeit limited, to both these markets. The new provision needs to be viewd as a significant step towards convertibility of the rupee on the capital account.
REQUIREMENTS FOR BOOKING FORWARD CONTRACTS EASED:

Currently, before booking a forward contract, authorised dealers need documentary evidence of the underlying exposire of the importer/exporter. In order to enable importers/exporters to book forward contracts on their expected payables/receivables, RBI has waived the requirement of documentary evidence before booking forward contracts. Authorised dealers can now book such forward contracts without any restriction on period on the basis of declaration of exposure. However, the total forward contracts outstanding at any point in time will not be allowed to exceed average external trade turnover of the last two years. This measure is expected to provide greater flexibility to corporates in managing their foreign exchange risks and will also help in the development of a fairly liquid forward market even beyond six months.
DEVELOPMENT OF RUPEE-FOREX MARKETS:

Several corporates having foreign exchange exposures arising out of external borrowings are unable to abtain long term forward covers and in turn opt for roll over their six month forward covers. This exposes them to considerable amount of foreign exchange risk. On the other hand there are certain corporates willing to swap their rupee liability into foreign currency liability. In order to enable these two types of corporates to hedge their foreign currency risks without altering India;'s external liability, RBI has permitted authorised dealers to run a swap book for such transactions without prior approval from RBI.
